questions.question: What is the scalar product of $19\mathbf i-4\mathbf j-6\mathbf k$ and $3\mathbf i+8\mathbf j-7\mathbf k$?
Given $\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, which of the following vectors is parallel to $\overrightarrow{AB}$?
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}=-3\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ (A).

questions.question: With a suitable substitution, $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/3}\tan^5x\sec^4x\,dx$ can be expressed as:
questions.answer: Let $u=\tan x$, $du=\sec^2x\,dx$, and $\sec^2x=1+u^2$. Then $\tan^5x\sec^4x\,dx=u^5(1+u^2)\,du=(u^5+u^7)\,du$. When $x=0$, $u=0$; when $x=\frac\pi3$, $u=\sqrt3$. So the integral is $\int_0^{\sqrt3}(u^5+u^7)\,du$ (B).

questions.question: For any two complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$, which of the following inequalities is always true?
questions.answer: The reverse triangle inequality: $|z_1+z_2|\ge\big||z_1|-|z_2|\big|$ (D). The others fail: for $z_1=z_2=1$, (A) is $0\ge2$ and (B) is $2\le0$; for $z_1=1,z_2=-1$, (C) is $2\le0$.

questions.question:
$f(x)$ is continuous, differentiable and integrable over its domain.
$\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}f(x)\cos x\,dx=2$, $f(0)=-1$ and $f\left(\tfrac\pi2\right)=3$.

Evaluate $I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}f'(x)\sin x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
By parts with $u=f(x)$, $v'=\cos x$: $\int_0^{\pi/2}f(x)\cos x\,dx=\Big[f(x)\sin x\Big]_0^{\pi/2}-\int_0^{\pi/2}f'(x)\sin x\,dx$.

So $2=f\left(\frac\pi2\right)(1)-f(0)(0)-I=3-I$, giving $I=1$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following functions does NOT describe simple harmonic motion?
questions.answer:
A function describes SHM if it can be written as $A\sin(nt+\alpha)+c$ (a single frequency).

(A) $4\sin^2t+3\cos2t=2-2\cos2t+3\cos2t=2+\cos2t$: SHM.
(B) both terms have frequency $3$, so they combine into one sinusoid $R\sin(3t+\beta)$: SHM.
(C) $5\sin4t+12\cos4t-3=13\sin(4t+\alpha)-3$: SHM.
(D) $3\sin5t-2\cos3t$ mixes two different frequencies, so it is periodic but not SHM (D).

questions.question:
A 3D shape is formed by placing two right prisms side by side, as shown in the diagram. One prism has a square base $ABFE$ and the other has a regular hexagonal base $EFILKH$. Both prisms have the same height, and all base edges have the same length.

Which of the following represents $\overrightarrow{DK}$?
questions.answer:
In the diagram, $\overrightarrow{AE}=\overrightarrow{DG}=\overrightarrow{BF}$, $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{EF}$ and $\overrightarrow{IL}=\overrightarrow{FH}$ (hexagon edges), $\overrightarrow{HK}=\overrightarrow{FI}$.

Option (C): $\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{HK}-\overrightarrow{AB}-\overrightarrow{FG}+\overrightarrow{IL}$. A route from $D$ to $K$: $\overrightarrow{DG}$ ($=\overrightarrow{AE}$), then $\overrightarrow{GF}$ ($=-\overrightarrow{FG}$, up the edge), then $\overrightarrow{FE}$ ($=-\overrightarrow{AB}$), then $\overrightarrow{EH}$ ($=\overrightarrow{IL}$), then $\overrightarrow{HK}$. So $\overrightarrow{DK}=\overrightarrow{AE}-\overrightarrow{FG}-\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{IL}+\overrightarrow{HK}$, which is (C).

Checking the others by components, none of (A), (B), (D) gives $\overrightarrow{DK}$; for example (B) $\overrightarrow{DG}+\overrightarrow{GJ}+\overrightarrow{IL}-\overrightarrow{KL}$ has the right horizontal displacement but its vertical displacement falls short of that of $\overrightarrow{DK}$ by one prism height.

questions.question: Which of the following best represents the parametric equation of the 3D curve shown?
questions.answer:
The curve stays within $|x|\le1$, $|y|\le1$ and its height satisfies $|z|\le\frac\pi2\approx1.6$ (the $z$-axis scale shows values up to about $\pm1.6$). Option C has $z=\arccos(\cos\pi t)$ ranging up to $\pi$, and option D has $y=\arccos(\cos\pi t)$ ranging up to $\pi$, so both are too large. That leaves A and B, where $z=\arcsin(\sin\pi t)\in[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]$.

Between A and B: the highest point on the curve is at positive $x$ (right-hand side); in B, $z=\arcsin(\sin\pi t)$ is at its maximum $\frac\pi2$ when $\sin\pi t=1$, i.e. at $x=\sin\pi t=1$. Also at $t=1$, B gives $(0,-1,0)$, which lies on the curve (A gives $(-1,0,0)$ there, which does not). So the answer is (B).

questions.question:
The intersection of four regions on the Argand diagram forms a kite with diagonals running along the real and imaginary axes. The regions are defined by:
$\arg(z-i)\le-\frac\pi3$, $\arg(z+i)\le\frac\pi3$, $\arg(z+\sqrt3)\le\frac\pi6$, $\arg(z+\sqrt3)\ge-\frac\pi6$.

What is the exact area of the kite?
questions.answer:
The kite has vertices at $i$ and $-i$ (on the imaginary axis) and on the real axis at the points where the boundary rays meet it.

Ray from $i$ at angle $-\frac\pi3$ meets the real axis where $\tan\frac\pi3=\frac1p$, i.e. at $x=p=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ (the same by symmetry for the ray from $-i$). The rays from $-\sqrt3$ at angles $\pm\frac\pi6$ meet the imaginary axis at $\pm1$ (since $\sqrt3\tan\frac\pi6=1$), consistent with the vertices $\pm i$, and the left vertex is at $-\sqrt3$.

Diagonals: vertical $2$ (from $-i$ to $i$), horizontal $\sqrt3+\frac1{\sqrt3}=\frac4{\sqrt3}$.

Area $=\frac12\times2\times\frac4{\sqrt3}=\dfrac4{\sqrt3}$ (B). (The open/closed boundary points do not affect the area.)

questions.question: $f(x)$ is a continuous and integrable function over the real numbers. Given that $f(2x)=3f(x)$ and $\displaystyle\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=2$, find $\displaystyle\int_1^2f(x)\,dx$.
questions.answer:
$f(x)=\frac13f(2x)$, so $2=\int_0^1\frac13f(2x)\,dx$. With $u=2x$, $dx=\frac{du}2$: $2=\frac16\int_0^2f(u)\,du$, so $\int_0^2f(x)\,dx=12$.

Then $\int_1^2f(x)\,dx=\int_0^2f(x)\,dx-\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=12-2=10$ (C).

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int2\cos5x\cos4x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
$2\cos5x\cos4x=\cos9x+\cos x$ (using $\cos A\cos B=\frac12[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]$).

$\int(\cos9x+\cos x)\,dx=\dfrac{\sin9x}9+\sin x+c$.

(The paper's solution writes the integrand as $\cos9x-\sin x$ and gets $\frac{\sin9x}9+\cos x$; that is incorrect.)

questions.question:
Write the number $1-\sqrt3\,i$ in modulus–argument (polar) form.

(The original paper asked for exponential form.)
questions.answer:
$|1-\sqrt3i|=\sqrt{1+3}=2$ and $\arg=-\frac\pi3$ (fourth quadrant, $\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\frac\pi3$).

$1-\sqrt3\,i=2\left(\cos\left(-\frac\pi3\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac\pi3\right)\right)$.

questions.question: Given that $1-\sqrt3\,i=2\left(\cos\left(-\frac\pi3\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac\pi3\right)\right)$, write $\left(1-\sqrt3\,i\right)^6$ in exact Cartesian form.
questions.answer: By de Moivre's theorem, $\left(1-\sqrt3i\right)^6=2^6\left(\cos(-2\pi)+i\sin(-2\pi)\right)=64(1+0i)=64$.

questions.question: Find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that the points $(-3,\alpha,\beta)$, $(5,4,2)$ and $(3,12,2)$ are collinear.
questions.answer:
The line through $(5,4,2)$ and $(3,12,2)$ has direction $(5,4,2)-(3,12,2)=(2,-8,0)$, so points on it are $(5,4,2)+\lambda(2,-8,0)$.

$x$: $5+2\lambda=-3\Rightarrow\lambda=-4$. $y$: $\alpha=4-8(-4)=36$. $z$: $\beta=2$.

So $\alpha=36$, $\beta=2$.

questions.question: Solve the quadratic equation $z^2-6z+13=0$ over the complex numbers, giving your answer in Cartesian form.
questions.answer: $z=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{36-52}}2=\dfrac{6\pm4i}2=3\pm2i$.

questions.question:
$O$ and $A$ are two points such that $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=5\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$.

Find the angle between $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ to the nearest degree.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}=5+4-12=-3$, $|\overrightarrow{OA}|=\sqrt{18}$, $|\overrightarrow{OB}|=\sqrt{50}$, so $|\overrightarrow{OA}||\overrightarrow{OB}|=\sqrt{900}=30$.

$\cos\theta=-\frac3{30}=-\frac1{10}$, so $\theta\approx96^\circ$.

questions.question:
$O$ and $A$ are two points such that $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf i+\mathbf j-4\mathbf k$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=5\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$, and the angle $\theta$ between $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ satisfies $\cos\theta=-\frac1{10}$ (with $|\overrightarrow{OA}||\overrightarrow{OB}|=30$).

Find the exact area of triangle $OAB$.
questions.answer:
$\theta$ is obtuse so $\sin\theta>0$: $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\frac1{100}}=\frac{\sqrt{99}}{10}=\frac{3\sqrt{11}}{10}$.

Area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{OA}||\overrightarrow{OB}|\sin\theta=\frac12(30)\frac{3\sqrt{11}}{10}=\dfrac{9\sqrt{11}}2$ square units.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^e\frac{(\ln x)^3}x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $u=\ln x$, $du=\frac{dx}x$; $x=1\to u=0$, $x=e\to u=1$.

$\int_0^1u^3\,du=\left[\frac{u^4}4\right]_0^1=\dfrac14$.

questions.question: Solve $z=\sqrt[3]{i}$, giving your answers in Cartesian form.
questions.answer:
$z^3=i=\cos\frac\pi2+i\sin\frac\pi2$, so $z=\cos\left(\frac\pi6+\frac{2k\pi}3\right)+i\sin\left(\frac\pi6+\frac{2k\pi}3\right)$, $k=0,1,2$.

$k=0$: $\cos\frac\pi6+i\sin\frac\pi6=\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac12i$.
$k=1$: $\cos\frac{5\pi}6+i\sin\frac{5\pi}6=-\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac12i$.
$k=2$: $\cos\left(-\frac\pi2\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac\pi2\right)=-i$.

questions.question: Shade the region in the complex plane defined by $1<\text{Im}(z)\le4$ and $\dfrac\pi4\le\arg(z)\le\dfrac{3\pi}4$.
questions.answer:
$\frac\pi4\le\arg z\le\frac{3\pi}4$ is the wedge above the origin bounded by the rays $y=|x|$ (including the rays). $1<\text{Im}(z)\le4$ is the strip above the line $y=1$ (excluded, dashed) up to and including $y=4$.

The region is the trapezium between $y=1$ and $y=4$ inside the wedge, with vertices $(\pm1,1)$ and $(\pm4,4)$: the boundary $y=1$ is dashed, the other three sides are solid.

questions.question:
A particle is moving in simple harmonic motion described by $\ddot x=-9(x-2)$. When the particle passes through the point $x=-1$ m its speed is $6\sqrt3$ m s$^{-1}$.

Find the distance the particle travels during a full period of its motion.
questions.answer:
The centre is $c=2$ and $n^2=9$. With amplitude $a$: $v^2=n^2\left(a^2-(x-c)^2\right)$.

At $x=-1$: $(6\sqrt3)^2=9\left(a^2-(-3)^2\right)\Rightarrow108=9a^2-81\Rightarrow a^2=21$, so $a=\sqrt{21}$ m.

In one full period the particle travels $4a=4\sqrt{21}$ m.

questions.question:
The points $A=(-1,0,0)$, $B=(0,1,0)$ and $C=(0,0,1)$ are three of the vertices of a regular unit octahedron centred at the origin.

Find $\text{proj}_{\overrightarrow{BC}}\overrightarrow{AB}$.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=2$.

$\text{proj}_{\overrightarrow{BC}}\overrightarrow{AB}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}}{|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2}\overrightarrow{BC}=\dfrac{-1}2\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\frac12\\-\frac12\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question:
The points $A=(-1,0,0)$, $B=(0,1,0)$ and $C=(0,0,1)$ are three vertices of a regular unit octahedron centred at the origin. It is known that $\text{proj}_{\overrightarrow{BC}}\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\frac12\\-\frac12\end{pmatrix}$.

Hence or otherwise find the shortest distance from $A$ to the line $BC$.
questions.answer:
The shortest distance is the length of the component of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ perpendicular to $BC$:

$\overrightarrow{AB}-\text{proj}_{\overrightarrow{BC}}\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\\frac12\\-\frac12\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\\frac12\\\frac12\end{pmatrix}$.

Distance $=\sqrt{1+\frac14+\frac14}=\sqrt{\frac32}=\dfrac{\sqrt6}2$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{2026}i^n$.
questions.answer:
Since $i+i^2+i^3+i^4=i-1-i+1=0$, every block of four consecutive powers sums to $0$. $2026=4\times506+2$, so the first $2024$ terms sum to $0$ and the remaining terms are $i^{2025}+i^{2026}=i+(-1)$.

Sum $=i-1$.

questions.question: Show that $x+\dfrac1x\ge2$ for all positive real numbers $x$.
questions.answer:
$\left(\sqrt x-\frac1{\sqrt x}\right)^2\ge0\Rightarrow x-2+\frac1x\ge0\Rightarrow x+\frac1x\ge2$.

(The paper's last line misprints '$\ge0$' for '$\ge2$'.)

questions.question:
Given that $x+\dfrac1x\ge2$ for all positive real numbers $x$, prove that for four positive real numbers $a,b,c,d$ with $a
e b
e c
e d$,
$$\left( rac ab- rac cdight)\left( rac ba- rac dcight)\le0.$$
questions.answer:
Expanding: $\left(\frac ab-\frac cd\right)\left(\frac ba-\frac dc\right)=1-\frac{ad}{bc}-\frac{bc}{ad}+1=2-\left(\frac{bc}{ad}+\frac{ad}{bc}\right)$.

With $x=\frac{bc}{ad}>0$, $x+\frac1x\ge2$, so the expression is $\le2-2=0$.

(Alternatively: $\frac ab-\frac cd=\frac{ad-bc}{bd}$ and $\frac ba-\frac dc=\frac{bc-ad}{ac}$, so the product is $-\frac{(ad-bc)^2}{abcd}\le0$.)

questions.question:
Use the substitution $u^2=5-x$, $u>0$ to show that
$$\int_1^4\frac3{x+4\sqrt{5-x}}\,dx=\ln\left(\frac{2048}{729}\right).$$
questions.answer:
$x=5-u^2$, $dx=-2u\,du$. When $x=1$, $u=2$; when $x=4$, $u=1$.

$\int_1^4\frac3{x+4\sqrt{5-x}}dx=\int_2^1\frac{3(-2u)}{5-u^2+4u}du=\int_1^2\frac{6u}{5+4u-u^2}du=\int_1^2\frac{6u}{(5-u)(u+1)}du$.

Partial fractions: $\frac{6u}{(5-u)(u+1)}=\frac A{5-u}+\frac B{u+1}$, so $6u=A(u+1)+B(5-u)$. $u=5$: $30=6A\Rightarrow A=5$. $u=-1$: $-6=6B\Rightarrow B=-1$.

$\int_1^2\left(\frac5{5-u}-\frac1{u+1}\right)du=\Big[-5\ln(5-u)-\ln(u+1)\Big]_1^2=(-5\ln3-\ln3)-(-5\ln4-\ln2)=5\ln4+\ln2-6\ln3$

$=\ln\frac{4^5\times2}{3^6}=\ln\frac{2048}{729}$.

questions.question: Consider the complex number $z=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta$. Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $z^n+\dfrac1{z^n}=2\cos n\theta$, $n\in\mathbb Z$.
questions.answer:
$z=\cos(-\theta)+i\sin(-\theta)$, so by de Moivre's theorem $z^n=\cos(-n\theta)+i\sin(-n\theta)=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta$ and $\frac1{z^n}=z^{-n}=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$.

Adding: $z^n+\frac1{z^n}=2\cos n\theta$.

questions.question: Let $z=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta$, so that $z^n+\dfrac1{z^n}=2\cos n\theta$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$. Hence or otherwise express $\left(z+\dfrac1z\right)^5$ in the form $A\cos5\theta+B\cos3\theta+C\cos\theta$ where $A,B,C\in\mathbb R$.
questions.answer:
$\left(z+\frac1z\right)^5=z^5+5z^3+10z+\frac{10}z+\frac5{z^3}+\frac1{z^5}=\left(z^5+\frac1{z^5}\right)+5\left(z^3+\frac1{z^3}\right)+10\left(z+\frac1z\right)$

$=2\cos5\theta+10\cos3\theta+20\cos\theta$.

So $A=2$, $B=10$, $C=20$.

questions.question: Given that, for $z=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta$, $\left(z+\dfrac1z\right)^5=2\cos5\theta+10\cos3\theta+20\cos\theta$ and $z+\dfrac1z=2\cos\theta$, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^5\theta\,d\theta$.
questions.answer:
$\left(z+\frac1z\right)^5=(2\cos\theta)^5=32\cos^5\theta$, so $\cos^5\theta=\frac1{16}\left(\cos5\theta+5\cos3\theta+10\cos\theta\right)$.

$\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^5\theta\,d\theta=\frac1{16}\left[\frac{\sin5\theta}5+\frac{5\sin3\theta}3+10\sin\theta\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac1{16}\left(\frac15-\frac53+10\right)=\frac1{16}\cdot\frac{128}{15}=\dfrac8{15}$.

questions.question:
A particle initially at the origin moves in a straight line with an initial velocity of $1$ m s$^{-1}$ such that its acceleration $a$ m s$^{-2}$ is given by $a=v\sqrt{4-v^2}$.

Find its exact velocity when its displacement $x=\dfrac\pi6$.
questions.answer:
$a=v\frac{dv}{dx}=v\sqrt{4-v^2}\Rightarrow\frac{dv}{dx}=\sqrt{4-v^2}$ (for $v>0$).

$\int_1^v\frac{dv}{\sqrt{4-v^2}}=\int_0^{\pi/6}dx\Rightarrow\left[\sin^{-1}\frac v2\right]_1^v=\frac\pi6$.

$\sin^{-1}\frac v2-\sin^{-1}\frac12=\frac\pi6\Rightarrow\sin^{-1}\frac v2=\frac\pi3\Rightarrow v=2\sin\frac\pi3=\sqrt3$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: A particle initially at the origin moves in a straight line with initial velocity $1$ m s$^{-1}$ such that its acceleration is $a=v\sqrt{4-v^2}$ m s$^{-2}$. With relevant mathematical reasoning, describe the eventual motion of the particle.
questions.answer:
Initially $v=1>0$ so $a=v\sqrt{4-v^2}>0$ and the velocity increases. From $\sin^{-1}\frac v2=x+\frac\pi6$, the velocity is $v=2\sin\left(x+\frac\pi6\right)$, which increases to $v=2$ at $x=\frac\pi3$, where $a=2\sqrt{4-4}=0$.

At $v=2$ the acceleration is zero, so the velocity stops increasing: the particle eventually moves at a constant velocity of $2$ m s$^{-1}$ (it never exceeds $2$, since $a\to0$ as $v\to2$ and $a>0$ for $0<v<2$).

questions.question: Find the exact volume of the solid formed when $y=\sqrt{2x\arctan x}$ is rotated about the $x$-axis, between $x=0$ and $x=\sqrt3$.
questions.answer:
$V=\pi\int_0^{\sqrt3}y^2\,dx=\pi\int_0^{\sqrt3}2x\tan^{-1}x\,dx$.

By parts with $u=\tan^{-1}x$, $v'=2x$ ($u'=\frac1{1+x^2}$, $v=x^2$):

$V=\pi\left\{\Big[x^2\tan^{-1}x\Big]_0^{\sqrt3}-\int_0^{\sqrt3}\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}dx\right\}=\pi\left\{3\cdot\frac\pi3-\int_0^{\sqrt3}\left(1-\frac1{1+x^2}\right)dx\right\}$

$=\pi\left\{\pi-\Big[x-\tan^{-1}x\Big]_0^{\sqrt3}\right\}=\pi\left\{\pi-\sqrt3+\frac\pi3\right\}=\dfrac{4\pi^2}3-\sqrt3\,\pi$ cubic units.

questions.question: Prove by contradiction that $4x^2-y^2=1$ does not have any integer solutions.
questions.answer:
Suppose there are integers $x,y$ with $4x^2-y^2=1$. Then $(2x+y)(2x-y)=1$.

Both factors are integers whose product is $1$, so either both equal $1$ or both equal $-1$.

If both are $1$: adding gives $4x=2$, so $x=\frac12$. If both are $-1$: adding gives $4x=-2$, so $x=-\frac12$.

In both cases $x$ is not an integer, a contradiction. Hence $4x^2-y^2=1$ has no integer solutions.

questions.question:
$OABC$ is a quadrilateral with $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$. $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $X$ is the point on $OM$ such that $OX:XM=n:1$. $X$ also lies on the line $AC$.

Express $\overrightarrow{OC}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and/or $\mathbf b$ in its simplest form.
questions.answer: $\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)+\mathbf a+\mathbf b=2\mathbf a$.

questions.question:
$OABC$ is a quadrilateral with $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$. $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $X$ is the point on $OM$ such that $OX:XM=n:1$.

Express $\overrightarrow{OX}$ in terms of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ and hence show that $\overrightarrow{AX}=\dfrac{n-1}{n+1}\mathbf a+\dfrac{n+2}{2(n+1)}\mathbf b$.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{OB}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AB}=2\mathbf a-\mathbf b$, so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OB}+\frac12\mathbf b=2\mathbf a-\frac12\mathbf b$.

Since $OX:XM=n:1$, $\overrightarrow{OX}=\frac n{n+1}\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{2n}{n+1}\mathbf a-\dfrac n{2(n+1)}\mathbf b$.

$\overrightarrow{AX}=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OX}=(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)+\frac{2n}{n+1}\mathbf a-\frac n{2(n+1)}\mathbf b=\frac{2n-(n+1)}{n+1}\mathbf a+\frac{2(n+1)-n}{2(n+1)}\mathbf b=\dfrac{n-1}{n+1}\mathbf a+\dfrac{n+2}{2(n+1)}\mathbf b$.

questions.question:
$OABC$ is a quadrilateral with $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$. $X$ lies on $OM$ ($M$ the midpoint of $BC$) with $OX:XM=n:1$, and $X$ also lies on the line $AC$. It is known that $\overrightarrow{AX}=\dfrac{n-1}{n+1}\mathbf a+\dfrac{n+2}{2(n+1)}\mathbf b$.

Find the value of $n$.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{AC}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathbf a+\mathbf b$. As $X$ is on $AC$, $\overrightarrow{AX}=\lambda(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$.

$\mathbf a,\mathbf b$ are not parallel, so equate coefficients: $\lambda=\frac{n-1}{n+1}$ and $\lambda=\frac{n+2}{2(n+1)}$.

$2(n-1)=n+2\Rightarrow n=4$.

questions.question:
What is the contrapositive of the following implication?
$$
eg(A\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow\left(
eg(A\Rightarrow B)\ 	ext{OR}\ 
eg(B\Rightarrow C)ight)$$
questions.answer:
The contrapositive of $P\Rightarrow Q$ is $
eg Q\Rightarrow
eg P$. Here $P=
eg(A\Rightarrow C)$ and $Q=
eg(A\Rightarrow B)\vee
eg(B\Rightarrow C)$.

$
eg P=A\Rightarrow C$, and by De Morgan $
eg Q=(A\Rightarrow B)\wedge(B\Rightarrow C)$.

Contrapositive: $\left((A\Rightarrow B)\ 	ext{AND}\ (B\Rightarrow C)ight)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow C)$.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1x(1-x)^n\,dx$ where $n$ is a positive integer. Show that $I_n=\dfrac1{(n+1)(n+2)}$.
Given that $I_k=\dfrac1{(k+1)(k+2)}$, by considering the partial fraction decomposition of $I_k$, find a closed-form algebraic expression for $S_n=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^nI_k$.
questions.answer:
$\frac1{(k+1)(k+2)}=\frac1{k+1}-\frac1{k+2}$ (from $1=A(k+2)+B(k+1)$: $A=1$, $B=-1$).

$S_n=\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)+\left(\frac13-\frac14\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{n+2}\right)=\frac12-\frac1{n+2}=\dfrac n{2(n+2)}$.

questions.question:
Use mathematical induction to prove that, for all positive integers $n$,
$$\tan\theta+2\tan2\theta+\cdots+2^{n-1}\tan\left(2^{n-1}\theta\right)=\cot\theta-2^n\cot\left(2^n\theta\right).$$
questions.answer:
Let $P(n)$ be the statement.

$n=1$: RHS $=\cot\theta-2\cot2\theta=\cot\theta-2\cdot\frac{1-\tan^2\theta}{2\tan\theta}=\cot\theta-\cot\theta+\tan\theta=\tan\theta=$ LHS. True.

Assume $P(k)$: $\tan\theta+\cdots+2^{k-1}\tan\left(2^{k-1}\theta\right)=\cot\theta-2^k\cot\left(2^k\theta\right)$.

Then for $n=k+1$: LHS $=\cot\theta-2^k\cot(2^k\theta)+2^k\tan(2^k\theta)=\cot\theta-2^k\left(\cot A-\tan A\right)$ with $A=2^k\theta$.

$\cot A-\tan A=\frac{\cos^2A-\sin^2A}{\sin A\cos A}=\frac{2\cos2A}{\sin2A}=2\cot2A$.

So LHS $=\cot\theta-2^{k+1}\cot(2A)=\cot\theta-2^{k+1}\cot\left(2^{k+1}\theta\right)=$ RHS of $P(k+1)$.

$P(1)$ is true and $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)$, so by induction $P(n)$ holds for all positive integers $n$.

questions.question: Use the fundamental theorem of calculus to show that $\dfrac d{dx}\left[\displaystyle\int_1^{x^2}\ln t\,dt\right]=4x\ln x$.
questions.answer:
Let $g(x)=\int_1^x\ln t\,dt$, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus $g'(x)=\ln x$. The given integral is $g(x^2)$.

By the chain rule, $\frac d{dx}g(x^2)=g'(x^2)\cdot2x=2x\ln(x^2)=2x\cdot2\ln x=4x\ln x$.

questions.question: Prove that the product of two consecutive positive even integers is divisible by $8$.
questions.answer:
Let the integers be $2n$ and $2n+2$ with $n\in\mathbb Z^+$. Their product is $2n(2n+2)=4n(n+1)$.

$n$ and $n+1$ are consecutive integers, so one of them is even and $n(n+1)=2k$ for some integer $k$. Then the product is $4\cdot2k=8k$, divisible by $8$.

questions.question: Given that the product of two consecutive positive even integers is divisible by $8$, prove that for all prime numbers $P>3$, $P^2-1$ is divisible by $24$.
questions.answer:
$P^2-1=(P-1)(P+1)$. $P>3$ is prime, so $P$ is odd, and $P-1$, $P+1$ are consecutive even integers, so their product is divisible by $8$.

Among the three consecutive integers $P-1,P,P+1$ one is divisible by $3$. $P$ is prime and greater than $3$, so $3\nmid P$, hence $3$ divides $P-1$ or $P+1$, and so $3$ divides $(P-1)(P+1)$.

$8$ and $3$ are coprime, so $24$ divides $(P-1)(P+1)=P^2-1$.

questions.question:
An exploratory lander on an exoplanet uses a magnetic launcher to fire a probe of mass $m$ kg vertically upwards. The launcher is positioned at $x=1$, where $x$ is the displacement from the surface in metres. The probe moves through a plasma atmosphere as it travels upwards under gravity $g$ m s$^{-2}$.

The combined net non-gravitational force $F_r$ acting on the probe is modelled by $F_r=\dfrac{mg}{x^3}\left(1+v^2\right)-mgv^2$, where $v$ is the speed of the probe.

Show that the equation of motion while the probe is moving upwards can be written as $\dfrac v{1+v^2}\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-g\left(1-\dfrac1{x^3}\right)$.
questions.answer:
Taking upwards as positive, the net force is $F_r-mg$ (gravity acts downwards), and $m\ddot x=mv\frac{dv}{dx}$:

$mv\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{mg}{x^3}(1+v^2)-mgv^2-mg=\frac{mg}{x^3}(1+v^2)-mg(1+v^2)=mg(1+v^2)\left(\frac1{x^3}-1\right)$.

Dividing by $m(1+v^2)$: $\dfrac v{1+v^2}\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-g\left(1-\dfrac1{x^3}\right)$.

questions.question:
A probe of mass $m$ is launched upwards from $x=1$ with initial speed $U$ m s$^{-1}$, where $x$ is the height above the surface. While moving upwards its motion satisfies $\dfrac v{1+v^2}\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-g\left(1-\dfrac1{x^3}\right)$.

Hence show that the greatest height of the probe $x=H$ satisfies $\ln\left(1+U^2\right)=2g(H-1)-g\left(\dfrac{H^2-1}{H^2}\right)$.
questions.answer:
Initially $x=1$, $v=U$; at the greatest height $x=H$, $v=0$.

$\int_U^0\frac v{1+v^2}dv=-g\int_1^H\left(1-x^{-3}\right)dx$

$\left[\frac12\ln(1+v^2)\right]_U^0=-g\left[x+\frac1{2x^2}\right]_1^H$

$-\frac12\ln(1+U^2)=-g\left(H+\frac1{2H^2}-1-\frac12\right)$

$\ln(1+U^2)=2g\left(H-1\right)+g\left(\frac1{H^2}-1\right)=2g(H-1)-g\left(\frac{H^2-1}{H^2}\right)$.

questions.question:
$A$ and $B$ are two distinct points in three-dimensional space such that $\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\8\\2\end{pmatrix}$.

Let $S_1$ be the set of all points $P$ such that $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{BP}=0$. Find the vector equation of $S_1$.
questions.answer:
Let $\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$. $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{BP}=(x-6)(x-4)+(y-4)(y-8)+(z+2)(z-2)=0$

$x^2-10x+24+y^2-12y+32+z^2-4=0\Rightarrow(x-5)^2+(y-6)^2+z^2=9$.

This is a sphere of radius $3$ centred at $(5,6,0)$ (the sphere with diameter $AB$: $M=(5,6,0)$ and $\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\frac12\sqrt{4+16+16}=3$).

Vector equation: $\left|\mathbf r-\begin{pmatrix}5\\6\\0\end{pmatrix}\right|=3$.

questions.question:
$A$ and $B$ are two points with $\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\8\\2\end{pmatrix}$. $S_1$ is the sphere $\left|\mathbf r-\begin{pmatrix}5\\6\\0\end{pmatrix}\right|=3$ (the set of points $P$ with $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{BP}=0$).

Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $S_2$ be the set of all points $N$ such that $|\overrightarrow{AN}|=|\overrightarrow{MN}|$. The intersection of $S_1$ and $S_2$ is the circle $S$. Find the radius of $S$.
questions.answer:
$M=(5,6,0)$ is the centre of $S_1$, and $|\overrightarrow{AM}|=3$. $S_2$ is the plane that is the perpendicular bisector of $AM$ (points equidistant from $A$ and $M$). It is at distance $\frac32$ from the centre $M$.

The plane cuts the sphere of radius $3$ in a circle of radius $r$ with $r^2=3^2-\left(\frac32\right)^2=9-\frac94=\frac{27}4$.

$r=\dfrac{3\sqrt3}2$.

questions.question: Show that $\displaystyle\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $u=a+b-x$, $du=-dx$. When $x=a$, $u=b$; when $x=b$, $u=a$.

$\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\int_b^af(a+b-u)(-du)=\int_a^bf(a+b-u)\,du=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)\,dx$ (the variable of integration is a dummy variable).

questions.question: Given that $\displaystyle\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)\,dx$, hence or otherwise find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\frac1{1+\sqrt{\tan x}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $I$ be the integral. Here $a+b=\frac\pi6+\frac\pi3=\frac\pi2$, so $I=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\frac1{1+\sqrt{\tan\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)}}dx=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\frac1{1+\sqrt{\cot x}}dx=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+1}dx$.

Adding this to the original: $2I=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\frac{1+\sqrt{\tan x}}{1+\sqrt{\tan x}}dx=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}1\,dx=\frac\pi3-\frac\pi6=\frac\pi6$.

So $I=\dfrac\pi{12}$.
